lessons.title: Skeletal and Muscular Systems
lessons.content:
The skeletal and muscular systems work together to provide support, protection, and movement for the human body. The adult skeleton consists of 206 bones, divided into the 'axial' skeleton (skull, vertebral column, and rib cage) and the 'appendicular' skeleton (limbs and girdles). Bones perform several vital functions: they provide a framework for the body, protect delicate organs (like the brain and heart), store minerals (calcium and phosphorus), and produce blood cells in the bone marrow.

Muscles are tissues that contract to produce movement. Skeletal muscles are usually attached to bones by 'tendons.' Because muscles can only pull and not push, they often work in 'antagonistic pairs' — when one muscle (the agonist) contracts, the other (the antagonist) relaxes. A classic example is the biceps and triceps in the upper arm: the biceps contract to flex the arm, while the triceps contract to extend it. There are three types of muscle: 'skeletal' muscle, which moves the skeleton and is under voluntary control; 'cardiac' muscle, found only in the heart, which contracts rhythmically and never tires; and 'smooth' muscle, found in the walls of organs such as the stomach and intestine, which works involuntarily.

Joints are where two or more bones meet. They are classified by the amount of movement they allow, such as 'ball-and-socket' joints (shoulder and hip) and 'hinge' joints (elbow and knee). Bones are held together at a joint by 'ligaments', strong bands of tissue that keep the bones in place and stop them moving too far apart. CSEC HSB students must be able to identify major bones and muscles and explain how they interact to facilitate movement. Understanding these systems is essential for discussing physical health and common injuries.
objectives: Identify major bones in the human skeleton
Explain the function of muscles and joints

experiment.description: The Skeletal and Muscular Systems: Match each structure to its function.

lessons.title: Circulatory and Respiratory Systems
lessons.content:
The human circulatory system consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood. Its functions are to transport oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products; to regulate body temperature; and to defend against disease. The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle. The septum separates the left and right sides, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

The pathway of blood: Deoxygenated blood from the body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (picks up oxygen) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Key points: the right side handles deoxygenated blood, the left side handles oxygenated blood. Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygenated, except the pulmonary artery); veins carry blood TOWARD the heart (usually deoxygenated, except the pulmonary vein).

Blood vessels: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pressure; veins have thinner walls with valves to prevent backflow; each heartbeat sends a pressure wave along the arteries, which is felt as the 'pulse' and can be counted at the wrist or the neck to measure the heart rate; capillaries are one-cell thick for efficient exchange of materials. Blood components: Red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), White blood cells (fight infection), Platelets (clotting), and Plasma (transports dissolved substances).
objectives: Identify parts of the human heart
Trace the path of blood through the body

experiment.description: Heart and Lungs: Arrange the route of blood through the heart and lungs in order.

lessons.title: Excretion and the Kidney
lessons.content:
'Excretion' is the removal from the body of the waste products made by the cells. The main excretory organs are the lungs (which remove carbon dioxide and water vapour), the kidneys (which remove urea, excess salts and excess water as urine) and the skin (which removes water and salts in sweat). Egestion, the passing out of undigested food as faeces, is NOT excretion, because that material was never absorbed into the body.

Urea is made in the 'liver' when excess amino acids are broken down (deamination). The blood then carries the urea to the 'kidneys'. Each kidney contains about a million tiny filtering units called 'nephrons'. In a nephron the blood is filtered under pressure, and useful substances such as glucose, some salts and most of the water are reabsorbed into the blood. What is left is 'urine', which passes down a 'ureter' to the 'bladder', where it is stored until it leaves the body through the 'urethra'.

As well as removing waste, the kidneys keep the water and salt content of the body steady: if you drink a lot, dilute urine is produced; if you sweat a lot, less urine is produced. Sweating also helps to control body temperature, because heat is taken from the skin when the sweat evaporates. CSEC HSB students must be able to name the organs of excretion and their waste products, and describe how the kidney filters blood and forms urine.
objectives: Identify the organs of excretion and the waste products each removes
Describe how the kidney filters blood and forms urine

experiment.description: Excretion: Match each organ to the waste product it removes.

lessons.title: The Eye and the Ear
lessons.content:
A 'sense organ' is a group of receptors that detects a particular stimulus and sends nerve impulses to the brain. The eye detects light, the ear detects sound and also helps with balance, the tongue detects chemicals in food through 'taste buds', the nose detects smell, and receptors in the skin detect touch, pressure and temperature.

In the eye, light first passes through the 'cornea', which refracts (bends) it as it enters. The 'iris' is the coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the 'pupil' and so the amount of light entering. The 'lens' focuses the light onto the 'retina' at the back of the eye. The retina contains 'rods', which work in dim light, and 'cones', which detect colour. Impulses then travel along the 'optic nerve' to the brain.

In the ear, the 'pinna' collects sound waves and the ear canal carries them to the 'eardrum', which vibrates. Three small bones pass the vibrations to the 'cochlea', a fluid-filled structure that converts them into nerve impulses for the brain. The three 'semicircular canals' lie above the cochlea and detect changes in the position of the head, which is how the ear helps us keep our balance. CSEC HSB students must be able to label the parts of the eye and ear and state the function of each.
objectives: Identify the parts of the eye and the ear
Explain how each part of the eye and ear helps us detect a stimulus

experiment.description: Sense Organs: Match each part of the eye or ear to its function.

lessons.title: The Endocrine System
lessons.content:
The 'endocrine system' is a set of glands that release chemical messengers called 'hormones' straight into the blood. Each hormone travels in the blood until it reaches its target organ, where a very small amount can produce a large effect. Hormone action is slower than a nerve impulse but lasts much longer, so the two systems work together to control the body.

The 'pancreas' produces 'insulin', which lowers blood glucose by converting glucose to glycogen for storage in the liver; a person who cannot produce enough insulin develops diabetes. The 'thyroid' gland produces 'thyroxine', which controls the metabolic rate - too little thyroxine causes a slow metabolism and, when the cause is a lack of iodine, a swelling of the neck called goitre. The 'pituitary' gland is often called the master gland: it produces 'growth hormone' and also controls the other glands. The 'adrenal' glands produce 'adrenaline', which prepares the body for action by speeding up the heart and breathing and releasing glucose into the blood.

Many hormones are controlled by 'negative feedback'. After a meal, blood glucose rises, so the pancreas releases insulin; glucose is stored as glycogen, and blood glucose falls back to normal. In the same way, thyroxine and adrenaline are only released when the body needs them. CSEC HSB students must be able to name the main endocrine glands, the hormone each produces and its effect on the body.
objectives: Identify the main endocrine glands and the hormones they produce
Explain how hormones such as insulin and thyroxine control body processes

experiment.description: Endocrine System: Match each gland to the hormone it produces and its effect.

lessons.title: Respiration and Energy Release
lessons.content:
'Respiration' is the release of energy from glucose inside living cells. It is not the same as breathing (ventilation), which is only the movement of air in and out of the lungs. The energy released by respiration is used for muscle contraction, growth, repair, and keeping the body warm.

'Aerobic respiration' uses oxygen and releases the most energy. Its word equation is: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy. The oxygen comes from the air in the alveoli, where oxygen 'diffuses' into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. During exercise the muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, so the rate and depth of breathing increase until the extra demand is met.

When the oxygen supply cannot keep up with very hard exercise, the muscles respire 'anaerobically': glucose is broken down without oxygen, producing 'lactic acid' and only a small amount of energy. Lactic acid builds up in the muscle and causes cramp and tiredness, and it must later be broken down using the extra oxygen we breathe in after exercise (the oxygen debt). CSEC HSB students must be able to distinguish aerobic from anaerobic respiration and state the word equation for each.
objectives: Distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
State the word equation for aerobic respiration and explain why breathing rate changes during exercise
concepts: Lactic acid and the oxygen debt
Diffusion of gases at the alveoli

lessons.title: Cell Structure and Function
lessons.content:
The cell is the basic unit of life. All living organisms are made of one or more cells. Eukaryotic cells, such as those in humans, contain specialised structures called 'organelles' that perform specific tasks. Key organelles include the 'Nucleus' (which contains genetic material), 'Mitochondria' (the site of energy production), 'Ribosomes' (where proteins are made), and the 'Cell Membrane' (which controls what enters and leaves the cell).

The human body contains many 'specialised cells' that are adapted for specific functions. For example, red blood cells are disc-shaped and lack a nucleus to maximise oxygen transport; sperm cells have a tail for swimming; and nerve cells are long and thin to transmit electrical signals over distances. Groups of similar cells working together form 'tissues,' and different tissues work together to form 'organs.'

In the CSEC HSB exam, you must be able to identify organelles in plant and animal cells and relate their structure to their function. You will also learn about the different levels of organisation in the body, from cells to tissues, organs, and systems. Understanding cell biology is the foundation for all other topics in human and social biology.
objectives: Identify organelles in plant and animal cells
Relate cell structure to function

experiment.description: Cell Structure: Match each cell part to its function.

lessons.title: Cell Division
lessons.content:
Cell division is the process by which cells multiply. There are two main types: 'Mitosis' and 'Meiosis.' Mitosis is used for growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction. It produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell, each with a full set of 46 chromosomes. This ensures that every cell in your body has the same genetic information.

Meiosis is a specialised form of cell division used only for 'gamete formation' (producing sperm and egg cells). It involves two rounds of division and produces four daughter cells, each with only half the number of chromosomes (23). Crucially, meiosis also involves 'genetic variation' through the shuffling of DNA, ensuring that offspring are genetically different from their parents and each other.

CSEC students must be able to distinguish between mitosis and meiosis and explain their significance. You will learn about the stages of the cell cycle and the importance of precise chromosome replication. Understanding cell division is essential for discussing topics like genetics, reproduction, and even how cancer develops when cell division becomes uncontrolled.
objectives: Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis
Explain the significance of cell division in growth and reproduction

experiment.description: Cell Division: Arrange the stages of mitosis in order.

lessons.title: Nutrients and a Balanced Diet
lessons.content:
Nutrition is the process by which we obtain the nutrients needed for growth, energy, and health. A balanced diet includes all seven essential nutrients in the correct proportions: carbohydrates (for energy), proteins (for growth and repair), fats (for energy and insulation), vitamins and minerals (for various body processes), fibre (for digestion), and water.

Malnutrition can occur if you get too little of a nutrient (deficiency) or too much (over-nutrition). For example, a lack of Vitamin C can lead to scurvy, while a lack of Iron causes anaemia. On the other hand, an excessive intake of fats and sugars can lead to obesity and related health problems like Type 2 diabetes. Different people have different 'dietary requirements' based on their age, sex, and activity level.

In the CSEC HSB exam, you will learn to identify the food sources and functions of each nutrient. You will also practise designing balanced meals and interpreting nutrition labels on food packaging. Understanding nutrition is vital for maintaining a healthy lifestyle and preventing chronic diseases.
objectives: Identify main food groups and their functions
Understand the impact of vitamins and minerals

experiment.description: Nutrients: Match each nutrient to its function in the body.

lessons.title: Digestion and Absorption
lessons.content:
Digestion is the process of breaking down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. It begins in the 'Mouth' with mechanical digestion (chewing) and chemical digestion (salivary amylase breaking down starch). The food then travels down the oesophagus to the 'Stomach,' where proteins are partially digested by gastric juices; the enzyme 'pepsin' begins the breakdown of proteins into shorter peptides.

Most digestion and nearly all absorption occur in the 'Small Intestine.' Here, enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver complete the breakdown of food. The inner surface of the small intestine is covered in tiny, finger-like projections called 'villi,' which greatly increase the surface area for efficient absorption. The remaining undigested waste then moves into the 'Large Intestine,' where water is reabsorbed before the waste is eliminated from the body. The 'appendix' is a small, finger-like tube attached to the caecum at the start of the large intestine; in humans it has no major role in digestion.

CSEC students must be able to describe the path of food through the digestive system and identify the specific enzymes involved (like amylase, protease, and lipase). You will also explore how factors like pH and temperature affect enzyme activity. Understanding digestion is key to understanding how our bodies obtain the energy and materials needed to survive.
objectives: Describe the stages of digestion
Identify the role of enzymes

experiment.description: Digestion and Absorption: Match each part of the digestive system to its role.

lessons.title: Teeth and Dental Health
lessons.content:
Digestion begins in the mouth, and the 'teeth' carry out the mechanical digestion that starts it. Each type of tooth has a job: 'incisors' cut, 'canines' tear, and 'premolars' and 'molars' crush and grind the food into smaller pieces. Humans have two sets of teeth - 20 milk (baby) teeth and, from about six years old, 32 permanent teeth.

A tooth is covered by 'enamel', the hardest substance in the body, which is made mainly of calcium salts. Beneath the enamel is the softer 'dentine', and in the centre is the 'pulp', which contains nerves and blood vessels. Enamel cannot grow back once it is worn away, so it must be protected.

'Tooth decay' starts when bacteria in the mouth feed on sugar from the diet and form a sticky film called 'plaque'. The bacteria turn the sugar into acid, and the acid slowly dissolves the enamel, opening a cavity that can reach the pulp and cause toothache. Tooth decay is prevented by brushing twice a day with 'fluoride' toothpaste, eating less sugar, and visiting a dentist regularly; fluoride hardens the enamel and helps it resist acid. CSEC HSB students must be able to describe the structure and functions of the teeth and explain how diet and dental care affect dental health.
objectives: Describe the structure and function of the teeth
Explain the causes of tooth decay and how it can be prevented

experiment.description: Teeth and Dental Health: Match each term to its description.

lessons.title: Vitamins, Minerals and Malnutrition
lessons.content:
'Vitamins' and 'minerals' are 'micronutrients': the body needs them in very small amounts, but they do not supply energy. They help enzymes work and keep the body healthy, and a shortage of one of them causes a deficiency disease.

'Vitamin A' (carrots, liver, green leafy vegetables) is needed for vision in dim light; a lack causes 'night blindness'. 'Vitamin C' (citrus fruits, guava, green vegetables) keeps gums, skin and blood vessels healthy; a lack causes 'scurvy', with bleeding gums and slow healing. 'Vitamin D' (sunlight on the skin, oily fish, eggs) helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth; a lack in children causes 'rickets', in which the bones stay soft and bend. Important minerals include 'calcium' (milk, cheese) for bones and teeth, 'iron' (liver, dark green vegetables) for making haemoglobin in red blood cells - a lack causes 'anaemia' - and 'iodine' (seafood, iodised salt) for making thyroxine, where a lack causes 'goitre'.

'Malnutrition' means a diet that is not balanced. Too little food, or too little protein, causes 'kwashiorkor' (severe protein deficiency, with a swollen abdomen, oedema and stunted growth) or 'marasmus' (a severe shortage of both energy and protein, causing extreme wasting and thinness). Too much food causes obesity, which increases the risk of diabetes and heart disease. CSEC HSB students must be able to link each vitamin and mineral to its function and to the deficiency disease it prevents.
objectives: Identify the sources and functions of the main vitamins and minerals
Explain the causes and symptoms of malnutrition, including kwashiorkor and marasmus

experiment.description: Micronutrients: Match each nutrient to the deficiency disease it prevents.

lessons.title: Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases
lessons.content:
Diseases are broadly classified into two categories. 'Communicable' (infectious) diseases are caused by 'pathogens' like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. These can be spread from person to person through air, water, food, or direct contact. Examples include malaria (spread by the Anopheles mosquito), dengue fever (spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito), cholera (spread by contaminated water and food), influenza, HIV/AIDS, and tuberculosis.

'Non-communicable' diseases are not spread by pathogens and are often related to 'lifestyle factors' and genetics. These include chronic conditions like diabetes, hypertension (high blood pressure), and many types of cancer. These diseases are now a leading cause of illness and death in the Caribbean, often linked to diets high in sugar and salt, lack of exercise, and smoking.

In the CSEC syllabus, you will learn about the causes, symptoms, and prevention of various diseases. You will also discuss the role of 'vectors' — organisms like mosquitoes, flies, and rats that carry pathogens from one host to another. Understanding these diseases is essential for promoting public health and making informed decisions about your own wellbeing.
objectives: Distinguish between types of diseases
Understand common disease vectors

experiment.description: Communicable or Non-communicable?: Sort each disease into the correct group.

lessons.title: Immunity and Vaccination
lessons.content:
The human body has several defence mechanisms to protect itself from disease. The first line of defence is the 'Skin barrier,' along with mucous membranes and stomach acid. If pathogens manage to enter the body, the 'Immune System' takes over. 'White blood cells' play a central role: some engulf and destroy pathogens directly, while others produce 'antibodies' — proteins that specifically target and neutralise different pathogens.

'Immunity' is the body's ability to resist a specific disease. It can be 'Active' (where your body produces its own antibodies, either after an infection or a vaccine) or 'Passive' (where you receive antibodies from another source, like a mother to her baby). 'Vaccinations' involve introducing a harmless form of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the immune system to produce memory cells, providing long-term protection.

CSEC HSB students must be able to explain how these natural and artificial defences work. You will also learn about the different types of vaccines and the importance of 'herd immunity' in protecting the entire community. Understanding immunity is vital for appreciating the success of public health programmes in eliminating or controlling infectious diseases.
objectives: Explain the body's natural defence mechanisms
Understand how vaccines provide protection

experiment.description: Immunity and Vaccination: Match each immune component to its function.

lessons.title: Water Supply and Pollution
lessons.content:
A clean water supply is essential for human health and survival. The 'Water Cycle' describes how water moves through the environment via evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. To make water safe for drinking, it must undergo several 'purification methods,' including sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination to kill harmful bacteria.

Environmental pollution occurs when harmful substances are introduced into the air, water, or land. Air pollution is often caused by the burning of fossil fuels, contributing to global warming and the greenhouse effect. Water pollution can result from industrial waste, sewage, or agricultural runoff. For example, 'Eutrophication' occurs when excess fertilisers enter water bodies, leading to algae blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish.

CSEC students will explore the sources and effects of various types of pollution and discuss ways to protect our natural resources. You will learn about the importance of sustainable water management and the measures taken by governments and organisations to reduce pollution and mitigate its impact on health and the environment.
objectives: Understand the water cycle and purification methods
Identify sources of environmental pollution

experiment.description: Water Purification: Arrange the steps of water treatment in order.

lessons.title: Waste Management
lessons.content:
Effective waste management is crucial for preventing disease and protecting the environment. Waste can be classified as 'Biodegradable' (can be broken down by decomposers, like food scraps) or 'Non-biodegradable' (cannot be easily broken down, like plastic or glass). Safe methods of disposal include 'Landfills,' 'Incineration,' and 'Sewage Treatment' for liquid waste.

As population growth increases, so does the volume of waste produced. This puts a strain on disposal systems and can lead to illegal dumping, which creates breeding grounds for vectors like rats and mosquitoes. To reduce the impact of waste, many communities promote the 'Three Rs': Reduce (use less), Reuse (use items more than once), and Recycle (process waste into new products).

In the CSEC exam, you will learn about the processes involved in sewage treatment and the importance of proper pit latrine and septic tank maintenance. You will also discuss the social and environmental challenges of waste disposal and the role of individuals and businesses in promoting sustainable waste management practices.
objectives: Describe safe methods of waste disposal
Understand the impact of population growth

experiment.description: Waste Disposal: Sort each waste item into the correct disposal group.

lessons.title: Substance Abuse
lessons.content:
A 'drug' is any substance that, when taken into the body, alters its function. While many drugs are used for medical purposes, 'Substance Abuse' occurs when drugs are used in a way that is harmful to the individual or society. Drugs are categorised based on their effect: 'Stimulants' (like caffeine or cocaine) speed up the nervous system, while 'Depressants' (like alcohol or heroin) slow it down.

Substance abuse has serious health consequences, including organ damage, addiction, and increased risk of disease. For example, smoking is a major cause of lung cancer and heart disease, while excessive alcohol consumption can lead to liver cirrhosis. Social consequences include broken families, loss of employment, and increased crime.

CSEC HSB students will study the physiological and social effects of various substances, including legal ones like tobacco and alcohol and illegal ones like marijuana and cocaine. You will also discuss the importance of education and support systems in preventing drug abuse and helping those who have become addicted. Understanding this topic is vital for making healthy choices and advocating for a drug-free society.
objectives: Identify types of drugs and their effects on the body
Understand the social consequences of drug abuse

experiment.description: Effects of Substances: Match each substance to its effect on the body.

lessons.title: Family Planning and STIs
lessons.content:
Family planning is the practice of controlling the number of children in a family and the intervals between their births. It is essential for the health of the mother and children and for the economic stability of the household. Various 'Contraceptive methods' are used to prevent pregnancy, including barrier methods (like condoms), hormonal methods (like the pill), and surgical methods (like vasectomy for men and tubal ligation for women).

Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) are infections spread through sexual contact. Common STIs include Syphilis, Gonorrhea, Herpes, and HIV/AIDS. While some STIs can be cured with antibiotics if caught early, others have no cure but can be managed with medication. Using condoms is an effective way to reduce the risk of contracting most STIs.

CSEC students must be able to describe different birth control methods and the symptoms and prevention of common STIs. You will also discuss the social and economic importance of family planning and the role of education and healthcare services in promoting reproductive health. This topic is a sensitive but essential part of the HSB syllabus.
objectives: Explain various birth control methods
Identify common sexually transmitted infections

experiment.description: Contraceptive Match: Match different birth control methods (e.g., barrier, hormonal, surgical) to their descriptions and effectiveness levels.

lessons.title: Human Reproduction and Development
lessons.content:
Reproduction is the process by which a new individual is formed. The male reproductive system produces the male gamete, the 'sperm', and the female reproductive system produces the female gamete, the 'egg' (ovum). 'Fertilisation' happens when a sperm fuses with an egg in the 'fallopian tube'. The fertilised cell is a 'zygote', which divides again and again as it travels to the uterus, forming a ball of cells called an 'embryo'. About a week later the embryo embeds itself in the lining of the uterus; this is 'implantation'.

The 'placenta' develops from the embryo and the lining of the uterus, and the 'umbilical cord' joins the developing baby to it. The placenta is the organ of exchange: oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother's blood to the baby, and carbon dioxide and other wastes such as urea pass from the baby to the mother to be excreted. The two blood supplies do not mix. The placenta also produces hormones that keep the pregnancy going, and it acts as a barrier against many, though not all, pathogens.

In the female, the 'menstrual cycle' lasts about 28 days and is controlled by the hormones 'oestrogen' and 'progesterone' from the ovaries. The lining of the uterus thickens, an egg is released at about day 14 ('ovulation'), and if the egg is not fertilised the lining is shed as 'menstruation'. The human life cycle is prenatal (conception to birth), infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age; 'puberty' is the stage of adolescence at which the body becomes able to reproduce. CSEC HSB students must be able to describe fertilisation and development and the role of the placenta.
objectives: Describe fertilisation and the development of the baby in the uterus
Explain the function of the placenta and the stages of the human life cycle
concepts: Puberty and the human life cycle

experiment.description: Human Development: Arrange the stages from fertilisation to birth in order.
